title: How Oobah Butler Scammed His Way to HBO
full_text: × HBO I meet Oobah Butler on a wet afternoon in Chinatown outside an empty claw-machine arcade. I spot the 34-year-old British hoax artist and gonzo journalist from way down the street, his platinum-blond mop top bobbing between umbrella-wielding tourists. The reason he picked this interview location — a few blocks from the open-air counterfeit handbag hub of Canal Street — becomes clear when he pulls out his phone. Giddily, he shows me a TikTok page called Clawmaster, an account dedicated to teaching followers how to win prizes out of these notoriously tricky arcade machines. Related Stories Robert Pattinson Is Officially James Bond: Meet the New 007 Actor 'The Odyssey' Returns to Imax 70mm Theaters Again After Record-Breaking Run “Let’s out-scam the scammers,” he says, grinning like the Cheshire Cat. We buy 50 tokens, and, as a bonus, the cashier lets Butler select from a mysterious deck of cards. Butler pulls from the top, revealing a Joker emblazoned with an anime character. She tells him he can redeem it later, so he slips it in his pocket. Butler sets his sights on a Charizard plushie, and we get to work. Scamming is Butler’s strong suit. Over the last decade, he’s gone viral a dozen or so times, pulling off stunts like listing bottles of Amazon drivers’ urine as an energy drink on the shopping platform and creating the Shed at Dulwich, an entirely fake restaurant that climbed to No. 1 in London on TripAdvisor. During a television press tour for the Shed, Butler auditioned lookalikes to do interviews in his place, fooling journalists around the world. Now, Butler is preparing to reveal five more fraudulent feats on his new HBO show, “Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow,” which debuts Sunday, Nov. 22. In the series, Butler immerses himself in the worlds of wellness, wine, music and online dating, and scams his way to the top. With a style somewhere between Nathan Fielder and Sacha Baron Cohen, Butler hilariously exposes the bullshit at the heart of our culture. An example: In the second episode, Butler takes smoke-tainted wine, which is considered so unsellable that vineyards distill it into hand sanitizer, and through clever manipulation and questionable marketing, earns endorsements from two of the world’s top sommeliers and the New York Times wine critic. By the end of the episode, he’s selling it for $500 per bottle. This penchant for scheming is in Butler’s blood. “My great-grandfather came to America in the late 19th century and was in the fur trade. It says in our family history that he used to sell rabbit droppings rolled in flour as medicine to people,” he says. “So I come from a long line of bullshit artists — or rabbit shit artists.” By this point, Butler and I have sunk at least 30 tokens into the claw machines with nothing to show for it. Marios, Pokémon and blue aliens in Italian soccer jerseys continue to slip our metal grasp, and we’re starting to doubt the Clawmaster’s expertise. Who is scamming whom? “He suggested that if you drop the claw right down into the hole, it loosens up,” Butler says. But none of the TikTok tips are working. See, Clawmaster never posts footage of him losing. And, also, he only works on machines where the claw dangles from an elastic cord; the machines here at Anime Claw are much more rigid, dropping down from a taut wire. “For God’s sake, this is infuriating!” Butler yells as another Charizard falls back into the pile. “Clawmaster fucked us.” Aside from a finale stunt six years in the making, Butler filmed nearly all of “Scams for a Better Tomorrow” in the last few months. He initially pitched the last episode — which is far too ambitious and surprising to spoil here — to A24 as a feature documentary, but the studio passed. Later, its television department reached out to Butler and said, “We want to make this a show.” With the help of Josh Safdie’s Central Pictures and “Nathan for You” production house Abso Lutely, Butler landed a pilot order at HBO, which would turn into a full series. The first episode sees Butler breaking into the wellness industry with a skin serum made of children’s tears. The influencers love it; Wall Street wants to throw money at it. A real New York dermatologist, after witnessing a group of kids crying into tubes, offers to endorse it — in exchange for a fee, of course. I ask Butler to define his ethics when it comes to duping people, but his eyes are lasered on a captive Jigglypuff. “Let me do this first, because that’s a harder question,” he says, chuckling. He misses. “We tried not to punch down,” Butler finally says. The joke is rarely on average people, but rather the highly awarded wine experts or the money-grubbing doctor. “I tried to be fair with people,” he says. Or, in the case of the dermatologist, “I’m being as fair as I need to be.” Still, Butler says it’s “a bit nerve-racking” that his subjects have yet to see the show. In the edit, he had to cut a few experts from the series, but “I’d have to go off the record to tell you why,” he says, “because it’s a legal thing.” Despite its puckishness, “Scams for a Better Tomorrow” is not so much a prank show. With each stunt, Butler seeks to reveal something deeper about human psychology. “Our argument in the wine episode is not that these guys suck because they fell for my trick,” he says. “It’s that the snobbery of that industry is getting in the way of the reality, which is this could be a good product.” HBO Butler was born Paul Arthur Butler, but his older sister nicknamed him Oobah as a baby. The name stuck, so much so that he legally adopted it in his early 20s. He grew up in Feckenham, a working-class English village of 700 people, and he credits his humble upbringing with instilling in him a confidence that would later come in handy. “I grew up with this sense that I could talk to anybody — it didn’t matter if it was the lord of the manor or the farmer down at the pub,” he says. “That gave me a sense of acting like I belong in any scenario. It’s a bit of a gift.” In his 20s, Butler sang and played guitar in a rock band, writing for music publications on the side. His band was so bad at selling records, he says, that it gave him an idea for an article. He would embed himself with the Jehovah’s Witnesses to learn their door-to-door marketing methods, but instead of hawking religion, Butler would go around peddling CDs. “I wanted to see if it was harder to sell music than God,” he says. In the battle of religion versus music, it turned out, music lost. He pitched the piece to Vice, which loved the idea, and the magazine brought Butler on as a freelancer. Soon enough he was writing regularly and making videos for Vice’s YouTube page that amassed millions of views. In a few years, Butler had leveraged his internet fame into a hosting gig on the British version of MTV’s “Catfish,” and he made two documentary features for the U.K.’s Channel 4. In 2024, like his rabbit-shit-peddling ancestor, Butler relocated across the pond. He arrived in the United States with no job and no plans. “I moved here on a whim and a feeling that my work would make sense here,” he says. “I found New York insanely inspiring.” America proved to be the perfect playground for “Scams for a Better Tomorrow.” “There’s so much more you can say here that you can’t say back home in the U.K.,” Butler says. “It’s harder in Europe to make claims about things. Here, you get a wider berth to scam — or market .” Case in point: He advertises that his dirt-cheap smoked wine is “Imported from Florence” but doesn’t exactly disclose that it’s simply been shipped to and from Florence, Massachusetts. “Inauthenticity is easier than ever now,” he says, mentioning the number of AI-generated commercials he endures while watching “Frasier” reruns. “I find it fascinating how comfortable we’ve become with it.” Throughout the show, Butler meets with Wall Street investors and tech founders who open their checkbooks and offer to fund his crazy ideas. I ask if he’s ever tempted to turn off the cameras and actually pursue one. “I find it really hard to be motivated by money,” he says. “It’s chasing the answer to questions, I suppose, that’s motivating to me.” HBO Fifty-nine minutes into the interview, we suddenly and shockingly win our first prize. Butler lets out a squeak of joy and we instantly embrace, examining the brown plushie — a drumstick with ears. “I think it’s, like, a chicken-bone bear,” Butler says. The next 15 minutes are wildly prosperous. Clawmaster-style, Butler and I shake the joysticks violently, securing a tuxedoed penguin, a polar bear with a yellow beanie and a miniature Kirby. But as we head toward the exit of the arcade, Butler realizes he never caught the one thing he truly wanted: the Charizard. He flashes his card at the cashier. “So what do I get with this?” “Any of the plushies,” she says, and Butler’s face lights up. She escorts us to the Pokémon machine and unlocks the cage. “This is America,” Butler says, smiling as he clutches his new black-and-red fire breather. “There’s always a Joker card.” Loading comments...

title: Joe Russo Talks ‘Doomsday’ Teaser-Trailer Strategy Ahead Of Rumored Monday Drop: “I Have To interact With Fans”
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Egyptian Music Star Mohamed Mounir Gets Biopic – Doha Industry Days ‘Al Hayba’ Star Taim Hasan To Play Syrian Whistleblower Farid Al-Madhhan In Neon-Backed ‘Caesar’ Biopic Steven Paul Talks Up Federal Film & TV Tax Credit: “It’s Going To Be Good For The World” – Industry Days Doha View All November 22, 2026 8:54am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Joe Russo Getty Images for Doha Film Festival Expectations that a new Avengers: Doomsday teaser or trailer is imminent have hit fever pitch over the weekend following cast member Hayley Atwell’s omission while signing autographs in New York that it is dropping on Monday (November 23). “There’s a new trailer dropping on Monday… am I allowed to have said that?” Atwell, who returns to the franchise as Peggy Carter, told fans on Friday night. Disney has also announced a sneak peek for November 30 during The Wonderful World of Disney: Holiday Spectacular on ABC, but this is believed to be a different tease. Related Stories News Watermelon Expands Production Ambitions As It Seals Partnership With Qatar's Film Committee News Egyptian Music Star Mohamed Mounir Gets Biopic - Doha Industry Days A few hours prior to Atwell’s omission, some 7,000 miles away in Qatar, co-director Joe Russo had also hinted at fresh drops before the picture’s opening by Disney on December 18, telling fans to keep checking their feeds. Watch on Deadline Talking in a fireside chat at the Qatar Film Committee ’s second Doha Industry Days, Russo explained that the four teasers, preceding an official trailer this summer, had played an integral role in the final version of the film. He said it had been a way to connect with the fans, which was essential because the audience landscape had changed so much since Avengers: Infinity War and Avengers: Endgame in 2018 and 2019 respectively. “I have to work extra hard to subvert your expectations and be aware of who you are as a viewer and how you’re changing,” said Russo. “The last time I did this, in 2018, 2019, is very different than now because we’ve been through a pandemic; lots of people spent a lot of time on social media. Movies saw a tremendous downturn, streaming saw a tremendous upturn, and now that all seems to be reversing. So, it shifts constantly,” he said. “You have to be a futurist to try to predict where the market is going.” “I have to interact with the fans in order to understand what is moving them, what is working for them,” he said. “What we’ve been doing with Doomsday is very different than the last time we did this because the speed of conversation on the internet is even faster than it was in 2018, 2019.” “I had this idea, why don’t we start the story a year early? Why don’t we start dropping clues in the year leading up to the movie… we did four trailers that were sprinkled out,” he continued. Kicking off on December 23, 2025, the first trailer showing Steve Rogers (Chris Evans) returning home, unpacking his Captain America suit, and holding a baby. A teaser on November 30 showed Thor (Chris Hemsworth) praying to Odin for strength. This was followed onJanuary 6 2026 drop featuring the X-Men and a January 13 teaser, featuring the Wakandans and Fantastic Four. “We’ve done a series of tags around the characters because the story actually started in January of last year, and you’ve been watching it slowly unfold and these are all pieces of something that are going to equal two and a half hours of your time on December 18,” he said. “It’s slowly investing them [fans] emotionally. But I’m also getting feedback as that’s happening and we can make adjustments as we go, based on what people are tracking or not tracking,” he continued. “It’s a very complicated story also, so I have to make sure that they’re following each little crumb we give them. If they get the wrong thing from it, then I have to make adjustments, knowing that they might have the wrong idea about it.” Talking about his return to the Avengers franchise alongside brother Anthony Russo, Joe Russo said he had been reluctant at first because of the immense challenge of pulling off a Marvel movie at that scale. He credited Robert Downey Jr., who played Tony Stark/Iron Man in Avengers: Endgame , with planting the seed for a return to the franchise, with his revelation that he was down to play Victor von Doom/Doctor Doom. “He’s a very dear friend of mine, but I also think he’s the greatest actor of his generation. This is a supremely talented, charismatic human being. And he translates incredibly well on a global scale. There’s something about the nature of his performance that translates,” said Russo. “There’s a style that belongs to these films that allows them to work in every market around the world. He just embodies that,” he said. Russo said Robert had gently enquired whether he was up for coming back to the Avengers franchise over dinner a couple of years ago. “I was still recovering from Infinity Wars and Endgame . And I was hesitant… he’s smart, he doesn’t push too much, he just kind of dropped the idea on the table and let it sit there, and then after dinner, he brought it up again, and I was like, ‘I don’t think I could do it, I’m still too tired.’ And then this festered for a little bit. And he didn’t even really tell me what he was going to do going back,” recall Russo. “And then another conversation happened where he said, ‘You know, I’m going to play Doom’. And I said, ‘That’s a really clever idea”. I can see a corollary there. There are thematics, greatest hero, greatest villain. There’s a multiverse. There’s a reason for being. There’s a compelling idea there. And I went, ‘Well, of course, who else could play the greatest villain other than you.” “It started to simmer in my brain a little bit. But we didn’t have a story. You can’t just show up with an empty canvas, so I still said no.” Russo credited longtime collaborator, screenwriter Steve McFeely, with coming up with the premise that gave a way in to writing Doomsday , after they had been pitching ideas back and forth. “Steve McFeely called me and said, ‘I have a crazy idea about how this works… what would happen if you left the cameras rolling at the end of Endgame ? What’s the very next scene that happens,” recounted Russo. “I said, “That’s really risky for a movie that had the level of success it did. You’re going to impact people’s emotional investment in it… this could blow up in your face,’ and then I went, ‘I love it’,” he continued. “The concept was like that’s a very happy ending for one character. And what if happiness is finite, and what if you have to take happiness from someone else to create your own happiness… What happens in that story? That’s where I went, ‘Right, I know what to do with this.” The idea that like there was a cost to a happy ending.” ‘Sunrise On The Reaping’ Opens To $120M NA; Franchise Returns To Fortune Netflix’s ‘Minimum Wage’ Ushers In Streaming’s Short Ep Sitcom Era Big Stars Coming To Heat Up Broadway’s Winter ‘Grand Theft Auto 6’ Speeds Aways With Nearly $4 Billion In Day 1 Sales Read More About: Comments

title: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping’ $225M WW Opening Bests ‘Wicked: For Good’ & ‘Michael’ – Sunday Update
full_text: Skip to main content By Anthony D'Alessandro Anthony D'Alessandro Editorial Director/Box Office Editor @AwardsTony More Stories By Anthony ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping’ $120M U.S. Opening Is Second Best Start For A Prequel After ‘Rogue One’; Lionsgate Franchise Returns To Fortune – Sunday Update ‘American Psycho’ Gets Axed: Luca Guadagnino Confirms His Adaptation Is “Not Happening” ‘Artificial’ Filmmaker Luca Guadagnino On Whether AI Is Humanity’s Doomsday & Sam Altman’s Arsenal – Crew Call Podcast View All November 22, 2026 8:50am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Joseph Zada is Haymitch Abernathy Lionsgate SUNDAY AM UPDATE: It’s the best opening for Lionsgate in quite some time as The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping minted $225M around the globe, $105M from 40,000 screens in 84 territories. That figure bests Lionsgate’s previous big opening of 2026, Michael which boogeyed to $218.8M in addition to last November’s pre-Thanksgiving blockbuster Wicked: For Good which debuted to $223M, the highest in that Broadway musical franchise. Those numbers are reported, not like-for-likes. Among all Hunger Games movies in the box office, the sixth title here (the fifth directed by Francis Lawrence) is the fourth biggest worldwide debut after 2013’s Catching Fire ($304M WW), Mockingjay Part 1 ($276.2M) and Mockingjay Part 2 ($241M) and ahead of the original Hunger Games ($214.2M). Sunrise on the Reaping is light years ahead of the global start of the previous Suzanne Collins novel, 2023’s Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes which debuted at $100.8M. Related Stories News 'Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping' Returns Lionsgate Franchise To Fortune With $120M+ U.S. Opening - Box Office Update Books 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping' Album Boasts 29 Songs; Releases Ahead Of Film The $120 million domestic opening is the fifth-largest domestic opening of 2026 among all studios. It is Lionsgate’s fifth-largest opener of all time. Watch on Deadline Internationally, 81 out of the 84 territories ranked No. 1. The top No. 1 territory debuts we have are: UK with $17.4M, the highest opening of the Franchise and in Lionsgate history. Australia counted $9.1M, Germany $8.4M, France was $7.1M (750,000 admissions), Mexico opened to $7M while China posted $5.9M. For Imax, Sunrise on the Reaping posted $26.4M around the global, the biggest opener for the large format exhibitor for the franchise. The pic was a Filmed for Imax title and was also Imax’s biggest global opening for a Lionsgate movie and Imax second best November global opening weekend of all-time. In North America, Sunrise on the Reaping took in $16.3M for Imax, repping 14% of the weekend and also the exhibits biggest November domestic opening weekend of all-time. Abroad, the Lawrence directed title counted $10.1M, repping 10% of the offshore debut. A total of 15 markets had IMAX top ten all-time opening weekends including Argentina, Australia, Belgium, Germany, Italy, and Netherlands. PREVIOUS FRIDAY EXCLUSIVE: Lionsgate’s sixth Hunger Games move, The Hunger Games: The Sunrise on the Reaping, is off to a strong start with $24.6M through Thursday night. Add that to the expected $51M Friday, which includes $21M in previews, and the global running cume is around $76M . Already, that’s close to toppling the previous $100.1M worldwide start of 2023’s The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes. The fifth Francis Lawrence directed movie in the Suzanne Collins franchise has opened to No. 1 in 66 out of 67 markets to date with another 17 territories set to bow this weekend. It would not be shocking if the movie files a global opening plus-or-minus $200M global. On Wednesday, the Joseph Zada, McKenna Grace, Elle Fanning, Jesse Plemons, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin ensemble pic bowed in France to No. 1 with 154,000 admissions or $1.4M, which was +157% ahead of Songbirds & Snakes. In Scandinavia, Norway on Wednesday, Sunrise opened to No. 1 with $494,000, marking the largest opening day in the Hunger Games franchise locally. Sweden opened to No. 1 with $459,000, coming in +31% ahead of Songbirds & Snakes . Belgium bowed to No. 1 as well with $343,000, the largest opening day locally for the feature take of the Collins’ novels. On Thursday, Haymitch set down in Australia with a No. 1 $1.5M opening for the day, +137% ahead of Songbirds and Snakes. Germany was also No. 1 with $1M, +83% ahead of Songbirds & Snakes. Lionsgate distributes their movies in Latin America with partner IDC. The series has always called at the B.O. there and combined all markets did close to $3M at No. 1. Of that, Mexico minted $1M, +107% ahead of Songbirds and Snakes, while Brazil grossed $679,000. Italy’s first day was also molto bene, +79% ahead of Songbirds & Snakes, for a No. 1 of $680K. In Scandinavia, Denmark bowed to No. 1 with $461,000, +65% ahead of the previous 2023 chapter. Finland was also No. 1 with $205,000 +36% higher than the Tom Blyth and Rachel Zegler starring installment. Netherlands charted No. 1 yesterday with $412,000, +66% over Songbirds & Snakes. In the Middle East, Sunrise on the Reaping bowed to first place in all markets with a combined $390,000. The UAE opened to $129,000, +135% ahead of Songbirds & Snakes . Saudi Arabia opened to $126,000 was also +155% ahead of the last Hunger Games movie. The net production cost of Sunrise on the Reaping is $150M, with a majority of that financed via foreign sales. title: Tom Jackson, Denver Broncos’ All-Pro Linebacker and ESPN Analyst, Dies at 75
full_text: Skip to main content By Mike Barnes Plus Icon Mike Barnes Senior Editor mikebarnes4 Follow Sign Up View All November 22, 2026 8:45am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Tom Jackson Streeter Lecka/Getty Images Tom Jackson, who parlayed a 14-season stint as a stalwart linebacker on the Denver Broncos’ famed “Orange Crush” defense into a career as a popular football analyst on ESPN , has died. He was 75. Jackson died Friday, his family told the network. No other details of his death were immediately available. Jackson was best known for his work alongside Chris Berman on the ESPN shows NFL Primetime and Sunday NFL Countdown , where the pair would deliver their humorous, entertaining take on highlights from games. Related Stories Music Peak Halftime Show: The A-List Machine Eventizing Pro Games Movies Lance Broadway, Pitcher Turned 'Olympus Has Fallen' Actor, Dies at 43 “All of us are stunned,” Berman said in a statement. “I’m stunned, we’re stunned and you’re stunned. We’ve lost one of the best human beings ever to walk the planet, Tom Jackson. I was fortunate to work side by side with Tom for 30 years … It was a labor of love for our whole team, both in front of the camera and behind it. We always hoped our viewers enjoyed the shows as much as we did bringing it to them every week.” Berman said on Sunday NFL Countdown that Jackson’s death was unexpected and that he had spoken with his best friend “at length” on Tuesday. “He was a vital 75,” he said. “Tom was so much more than an accomplished NFL analyst,” he said in his statement. “There was nobody kinder, more thoughtful, more loyal or more engaging than him. And when it came to laughter, Tom’s was frequent and unmistakable. He is easily summed up by this classic old song: ‘He’s got sunshine on a cloudy day.’” Added ESPN chairman Jimmy Pitaro: “He brought the credibility of an All-Pro NFL player, the insight of a gifted analyst and a warmth and authenticity that connected with generations of football fans.” ESPN’s NFL studio is named the Chris Berman-Tom Jackson Studio. Born in Cleveland on April 4, 1951, Thomas Louie Jackson attended John Adams High School in the city before he was recruited by University of Louisville head coach Lee Corso — another future ESPN commentator — to join the Cardinals. A fourth-round pick (88th overall) by the Broncos in the 1973 NFL Draft, he played in 191 regular-season games, the most in team history when he retired in 1986, and 10 playoff games, all with Denver. He was a first-team All-Pro in 1977 and 1978 and a three-time Pro Bowl selection and inducted into the team’s Ring of Fame in 1992. When he retired at 36, Jackson was the NFL’s oldest linebacker. “An inspirational leader and fierce competitor, TJ was a proud member of the Broncos’ first Super Bowl team [in 1977] that helped establish a winning tradition in Denver,” the team said in a statement. “Off the field, Tom carried himself with class, warmth and humility, forging deep connections and lifelong friendships with teammates and throughout Broncos Country.” Jackson, who joined ESPN in 1987, was awarded the Pete Rozelle Radio-Television Award by the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2015. He retired from broadcasting a year later but reunited with Berman for a digital-only edition of NFL Primetime in 2019. He often said that he had been “blessed to work for two companies in my life: the Denver Broncos and ESPN.” Survivors include his wife, Jennifer, and his daughters, Taylor and Morgan. THR

title: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Slays $120M at Box Office as Franchise Heats Back Up
full_text: × Skip to main content By Ryan Gajewski Plus Icon Ryan Gajewski Senior Entertainment Reporter View All November 22, 2026 8:44am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Joseph Zada (left) and Elle Fanning in 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.' Courtesy of Everett Collection Logo text The Hunger Games franchise has been revived at the box office . Meanwhile, I Play Rocky demonstrated major strength as it expanded wide with a rare A+ CinemaScore, and Elsinore notched a promising per-screen average in limited release. Lionsgate released The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping in 4,018 North American theaters, and the sixth film in the dystopian franchise grossed $120 million in its opening weekend. This gives it the fourth-best debut in franchise history, besting 2015’s second Mockingjay movie ($102.6 million) and 2023 prequel The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes ($44.6 million) but behind 2013’s Catching Fire ($158 million), 2012’s series-launching The Hunger Games ($152.5 million) and 2014’s first Mockingjay ($121.8 million). Its $56 million domestic sum on Friday gave Sunrise the third-best debut Friday in franchise history, behind Catching Fire and The Hunger Games . Related Stories Movies How 'I Play Rocky' Star P.J. Byrne Became One of Hollywood's Go-To Character Actors Beyond the Book "The Secrecy Was Insane:" The Making of 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,' From Locked Safes to Original Cast's Return The new film added $105 million from 84 international territories for a global haul of $225 million. Its audience was 67 percent female, with 50 percent of the crowd above age 25, according to PostTrak. Sunrise earned an A- CinemaScore from audiences, putting it below the A grades of the Jennifer Lawrence -led initial 2012 movie that kicked off the series and 2013’s Catching Fire but matching the A- grades of the two Mockingjay films. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping will notch the fifth-biggest opening in Lionsgate history, as it also stands at No. 5 among 2026 domestic openings for all studios. It represents the highest-grossing launch for the careers of stars Glenn Close, Jesse Plemons, Kieran Culkin and Elle Fanning. This weekend’s haul also brings the Hunger Games franchise’s box office total to roughly $3.437 billion to make it the studio’s highest-grossing franchise ever, topping The Twilight Saga . Jesse Plemons in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping . Murray Close / Lionsgate /Courtesy Everett Collection Lionsgate had projected The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping to gross north of $80 million , but other sources expected that it would collect between $100 million and $130 million. Adapting author Suzanne Collins’ prequel novel that was published last year, director Francis Lawrence ‘s movie carries a production budget of roughly $150 million as it revitalizes the franchise by telling a story set 24 years before the events of Collins’ original 2008 book. This opening represents a major comeback for the series after registering its lowest-performing entry with 2023 prequel The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes , given that Sunrise on the Reaping opened with more than double its launch. Starring Tom Blyth, Rachel Zegler and Hunter Schafer, Songbirds & Snakes — telling the backstory for the villainous President Snow, played by Ralph Fiennes in the new movie — disappointed, opening to $44 million domestically for the weekend before ending its run with $166.4 million domestically and a global sum of $361.8 million. It earned a B+ CinemaScore, the lowest for the franchise. “When you have filmmaking giants as talented as Francis Lawrence [and producers] Nina Jacobson and Brad Simpson guiding the vision established by the brilliant creator Suzanne Collins, who started it all, you are in enormously capable hands,” Lionsgate film chief Adam Fogelson said in a statement. “This success is a testament to their remarkable film, the performances of our incredibly talented cast, and ultimately, the love of Hunger Games fans worldwide, who embraced a film that told a story they had been asking to see for many years.” Joseph Zada and Whitney Peak in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping. Murray Close /Lionsgate / Courtesy Everett Collection Sunrise on the Reaping holds a 67 percent critical score on Rotten Tomatoes, lagging behind the franchise’s first four movies but besting the 64 percent approval for Songbirds & Snakes . The new film has a franchise-best 95 audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. In his review for The Hollywood Reporter , chief film critic David Rooney wrote that it “delivers on emotion and brutal spectacle.” The movie opened the day after the launch of the hotly anticipated video game Grand Theft Auto 6 , which did not appear to prevent the film from thriving. Joseph Zada stars as Haymitch Abernathy, providing the backstory for the character whom Woody Harrelson brought to life in the first four movies. The cast for Sunrise on the Reaping also includes Mckenna Grace, Whitney Peak and Maya Hawke. Among other weekend titles, Amazon MGM Studios expanded I Play Rocky to 2,477 North American locations after two frames in limited release. Peter Farrelly’s Rocky origin story earned a healthy $9.3 million to bring its domestic total to $10.4 million. The crowd skewed male at 56 percent, as 33 percent of moviegoers were age 55 and above. Starring Anthony Ippolito as a young Sylvester Stallone, I Play Rocky landed a rare A+ CinemaScore, becoming only the second release this year to do so (after April’s A Great Awakening ). I Play Rocky holds an 89 percent approval rating from critics on Rotten Tomatoes and a 98 percent audience score. Rooney’s review described it as a “big-hearted movie about moviemaking, if not an artful one.” Anthony Ippolito and Stephan James in I Play Rocky. Claire Folger/Amazon Content Services In its sophomore frame, Paramount’s horror-tinged holiday offering Ebenezer claimed third place with roughly $7.7 million for a decline of around 59 percent, bringing its domestic cume to $32.5 million. Johnny Depp marks his studio comeback vehicle with director Ti West’s reimagining of Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol , which opened atop last weekend’s box office. Continuing to draw families in its third weekend is Warner Bros.’ The Cat in the Hat , as the animated adaptation of Dr. Seuss’ classic children’s book grossed around $6.9 million for a domestic total of $47.1 million. title: Box Office: ‘Sunrise on the Reaping’ Reignites ‘Hunger Games’ Franchise With $120 Million Debut
full_text: × Nov 22, 2026 8:16am PT Box Office: ‘Sunrise on the Reaping’ Reignites ‘Hunger Games’ Franchise With $120 Million Debut By Rebecca Rubin Plus Icon Rebecca Rubin Senior Film and Media Reporter rebeccaarubin Latest Barack and Michelle Obama’s Higher Ground to Produce Off-Broadway Revival of ‘Rumors’ Led By ‘Real Housewives’ Stars (EXCLUSIVE) 3 days ago NHL Legend Tie Domi to Launch ‘Keeping It Real with Tie’ Interview Series With Tom Brady as First Guest 4 days ago Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Targets Huge Debut Above $100 Million 4 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source ©Lions Gate/Courtesy Everett Collection “Sunrise on the Reaping” caught fire at the domestic box office, collecting a sensational $120 million in its opening weekend while reinvigorating Lionsgate’s “Hunger Games” franchise. Overseas, “Sunrise on the Reaping” generated $105 million from 84 territories for a towering launch of $225 million globally. The dystopian prequel is one of just five movies this year to launch above $100 million in North America, joining the company of “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” ($360 million), “Toy Story 5” ($159 million), “The Super Mario Galaxy Movie” ($131 million) and “The Odyssey” ($123 million). All of those films eventually surpassed the $1 billion mark globally. Rockstar’s video game “Grand Theft Auto VI” launched after years of anticipation, earning a staggering $3.79 billion on its first day . It’s expected to set a sales record for entertainment across any medium. “Many have speculated as to whether the release of ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ would hurt ‘The Hunger Games’ at the box office, and I think the marketplace has already spoken,” adds Dergarabedian. “There’s plenty of time to play ‘GTA VI’ and make it to a theater to see ‘Sunrise on the Reaping’ this weekend.” On top of pitched competition at home, initial ticket sales for “Sunrise on the Reaping” are notable because they’re not far off from the original saga. For reference, 2012’s “The Hunger Games” ignited to $152 million, followed by 2013’s “Catching Fire” ($158 million), 2014’s “Mockingjay Part 1” ($121 million) and 2015’s “Mockingjay Part 2” ($102 million). Nearly a decade after those movies, starring Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson, concluded their run, the studio revived the young-adult property with 2023’s “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes,” an origin story about Panem’s cruel leader, President Coriolanus Snow. That film, set during the 10th Hunger Games, bowed significantly below its predecessors with $44 million. However, the movie stuck around through the holidays and eventually climbed to $363 million globally, registering as a win against a (comparatively leaner) $100 million budget and justifying another prequel for the studio. “Sunrise on the Reaping,” which returns to Panem for the 50th Hunger Games, carries a larger price tag above $150 million, not including the many millions spent on worldwide marketing efforts. That “Sunrise on the Reaping” managed to recapture the spark of the initial series is impressive as the sixth installment in any property. And the film earned a strong “A-” grade on CinemaScore exit polls, which bodes well for box office longevity. Analysts attribute the strong debut to several factors, including the franchise’s multi-generational appeal as well as the excitement for the return of fan-favorite characters. This chapter, based on the novel by Suzanne Collins, has a stronger connection to the original saga; the story follows a young Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada takes on the role originally played by Woody Harrelson) — who eventually mentors Katniss (Lawrence) and Peeta (Hutcherson) in their Hunger Games, a Battle Royale for teens. Francis Lawrence returned to direct, having helmed all but the first chapter in the YA-centric franchise. “The last ‘Hunger Games’ stumbled when the story went back 64 years without Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson and Woody Harrelson,” says David A. full_text: Skip to main content By Anthony D'Alessandro Anthony D'Alessandro Editorial Director/Box Office Editor @AwardsTony More Stories By Anthony ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping’ $120M U.S. Opening Is Second Best Start For A Prequel After ‘Rogue One’; Lionsgate Franchise Returns To Fortune – Sunday Update ‘American Psycho’ Gets Axed: Luca Guadagnino Confirms His Adaptation Is “Not Happening” ‘Artificial’ Filmmaker Luca Guadagnino On Whether AI Is Humanity’s Doomsday & Sam Altman’s Arsenal – Crew Call Podcast View All November 22, 2026 7:38am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Joseph Zada in 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' Lionsgate/Everett Collection SUNDAY AM: Lionsgate and Suzanne Collins accomplished what no other Harry Potter movie has pulled off at the box office: Seeing a preview/spinoff opening to north of $100M at the domestic B.O., which is exactly what their Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping did with a North American start of $120M. In addition, Sunrise on the Reaping ranks as the second best U.S./Canada opening for a prequel after 2016’s Rogue One: A Star Wars Story which debuted to $155M. This is also Lionsgate’s biggest opening post Covid, and their first $100M+ opening in 11 years, the last being 2015’s The Hunger Games: Mockingjay Part 2 with $102.66M. As rich as Harry Potter was in its sequels, Warners wasn’t able to get Fantasti c Beasts to shine greater than a $74.4M opening, which is what the first prequel/spinoff title opened to in 2016. Hence, the Fantastic Beast movies became industry comps (along with 2019’s Hobbs & Shaw with a $60M start) in regards to the ceilings of what a spinoff/prequel franchise could open to at the box office. The reason why we’re banging this drum is because when Lionsgate opened The Hunger Games: Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes to a ho-hum $44.6M three years ago, it felt like the popularity of the Collins franchise had hit the bottom of the well, destined to live in a middling range for the rest of its days. Nope. Thumbs up to Collins for getting the franchise back on track in the backstory of Woody Harrelson character Haymitch Abernathy, making the sixth novel in the 14-year old series feel like the biggest Games yet, and to Lionsgate Motion Picture Chairman Adam Fogelson in the continued belief that Hunger Games could see a renaissance among its fanship. It also helped that Collins’ latest novel Sunrise on the Reaping sold way more, and was received with more warmth than Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes which debuted during Covid . Said Fogelson, “When you have filmmaking giants as talented as Francis Lawrence, Nina Jacobson, and Brad Simpson guiding the vision established by the brilliant creator Suzanne Collins, who started it all, you are in enormously capable hands. This success is a testament to their remarkable film, the performances of our incredibly talented cast, and ultimately, the love of Hunger Games fans worldwide, who embraced a film that told a story they had been asking to see for many years. Because of the incredible work of every part of our Motion Picture Group and our amazing filmmaking team, combined with the passion and devotion of the Hunger Games family of fans, the franchise is as strong and vibrant today as when the first Hunger Games film was released nearly 15 years ago.” How Lionsgate got Sunrise on the Reaping to shine brighter than the sun: That teaser, which launched a year ago, was the second most-watched in the studio’s history after Michael with 109M global views in its first 24-hours. If you want to bridge the gap in a legacy franchise between old fans and a new generation, you have to honor the old with the new. As such, to make fans go bananas, it was leaked back in December that OG Hunger Games stars Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson were reprising their characters in the prequel — a scene that fans were also treated to in the book. Lionsgate leaned into them and Harrelson in the marketing with appearances on The Tonight Show and Watch What Happens Live. When Lionsgate announced the 16 individual castings, those yielded 541 million views and 35.2 million engagements, an early driver and indicator of fans excitement. The top movie titles where the trailer was previewed in-theaters included Spider-Man: Brand New Day, Michael and The Housemaid. title: ‘The Unknown’ Director Arthur Harari Says AI Is a ‘Slippery Slope,’ Though He ‘Had to Use Deepfake Tool’ for Léa Seydoux Double Scene: ‘There Was a Human Behind It’
full_text: × Nov 22, 2026 7:02am PT ‘The Unknown’ Director Arthur Harari Says AI Is a ‘Slippery Slope,’ Though He ‘Had to Use Deepfake Tool’ for Léa Seydoux Double Scene: ‘There Was a Human Behind It’ By Christopher Vourlias Plus Icon Christopher Vourlias Latest ‘The Unknown’ Director Arthur Harari Says AI Is a ‘Slippery Slope,’ Though He ‘Had to Use Deepfake Tool’ for Léa Seydoux Double Scene: ‘There Was a Human Behind It’ 2 hours ago Marrakech’s Atlas Workshops Takes Victory Lap as Industry Event Celebrates Cannes, Venice Triumphs 4 days ago Marrakech Film Festival Grows Its Awards-Season Clout With ‘Artificial,’ ‘The Debut,’ ‘Fjord’ and Other Oscar Hopefuls 4 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Gareth Cattermole “ The Unknown ” filmmaker Arthur Harari says AI is a “slippery slope” and one he’d prefer to avoid in his own work — even as he admitted on Sunday at the Marrakech Film Festival that he used a deepfake tool in his Palme d’Or contender, a body-swap psychodrama starring Léa Seydoux. Appearing in conversation with film critic and historian Charles Tesson, the Oscar-winning “Anatomy of a Fall” co-writer was asked by an audience member how he viewed the role of AI technology in his creative process. Related Stories Zendaya Felt ‘Incredibly Nervous’ While Shooting ‘The Odyssey’ but Credits Tom Holland for Supporting Her: He Was ‘in the Corner Like, “You Got This”’ Robert Pattinson Said in 2012 That He'd 'Definitely' Want to Be James Bond in 'Like 20 Years' When He's Not So 'Fresh-Faced' “I’m in much the same position as everyone else: this shift toward using AI is suddenly upon us, and it’s becoming not just a possibility, but something increasingly pervasive and tempting,” Harari said. “Personally, I’ve never used it; for the time being, I don’t see any place for it in my work.” The acclaimed writer-director went on to walk that statement back moments later, when he admitted that his team employed deepfake technology for a pivotal scene in his latest film. “At one point in ‘The Unknown,’ there is a scene where Léa Seydoux kisses Léa Seydoux, and we had to use a deepfake tool to do that,” he said. “But there was a human behind it. There was always a human involved — someone who programs it, so to speak, and keeps it under control. So, I’m not against it in principle. It’s just that I think we need to ask ourselves what constitutes the essence of what we’re trying to create — right from the writing stage.” As a writer, Harari appeared to be more resistant to the technology, conceding that AI tools were “perfectly legitimate and interesting” when it comes to performing simple research tasks. But to go beyond that — “to actually craft parts of the writing process” — was, he insisted, “a very slippery slope.” “The thing is, we are inherently prone to addiction — look at our phones, for instance; we’re constantly glued to them,” he said. “Once you get a foot in the door, it becomes incredibly difficult not to use it at every turn.” Premiering in competition at this year’s Cannes Film Festival, “The Unknown” stars Seydoux as an unknown woman who has a one-night stand with a photographer named David (Niels Schneider). When David wakes up, he’s trapped inside Seydoux’s body. The film was based on a graphic novel co-written by Harari. Speaking to Variety earlier this year, the French actress described the role as “the best part I’ve ever played.” Asked if she thought AI would put filmmakers out of business, she replied, “I don’t think so. I think that nothing can replace humanity. I don’t feel threatened. Maybe I’m wrong! But I believe in human nature.” Harari is on hand at the Marrakech Film Festival as part of its popular Conversation series. He’s appearing alongside “Knives Out” director Rian Johnson, “Call Me by Your Name” Oscar nominee Luca Guadagnino, “Fjord” Palme d’Or winner Cristian Mungiu, Italian screen icon Monica Bellucci and more. The Marrakech Film Festival runs Nov. 20–28. title: J.A. Bayona, Guneet Monga Kapoor, Vikas Khanna Board Student Academy Award Winner ‘The Dragon Letter’ as Director Plans Feature Version (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: × Nov 22, 2026 6:25am PT J.A. Bayona, Guneet Monga Kapoor, Vikas Khanna Board Student Academy Award Winner ‘The Dragon Letter’ as Director Plans Feature Version (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest J.A. Bayona, Guneet Monga Kapoor, Vikas Khanna Board Student Academy Award Winner ‘The Dragon Letter’ as Director Plans Feature Version (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago Karla Sofia Gascon Says ‘Emilia Perez’ Oscar Controversy Came From People Who ‘Didn’t Want Someone Like Me to Receive an Award’ 9 hours ago Oscar-Winning Doc ‘The Elephant Whisperers’ Co-Writer’s Dark Comedy ‘Nose Bone’ Follows a Punjabi Woman’s Race for an Abortion at WAVES Film Bazaar 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Sikhya Entertainment Spanish director J.A. Bayona , Oscar-winning producer Guneet Monga Kapoor and Michelin-starred chef and filmmaker Vikas Khanna have come aboard short “The Dragon Letter” as executive producers, and Ladakhi director Stanzin Jigmet tells Variety he is developing a feature version of the Student Academy Award-winning short. The film was named the narrative Gold winner at the 53rd Student Academy Awards, and has been entered in the live action short race for the 99th Academy Awards. Spain’s ESCAC Films produced it in association with India Sikhya Entertainment, with shooting split between Ladakh and Barcelona. Related Stories 'The Odyssey,' 'Dune 3,' 'Michael' and More Top Artisans Honored at Hamilton Behind the Camera Awards A Version of Zendaya's Viral 'Spider-Man' Tee Is Now Available to Shop Online Bayona was born in Barcelona, the city where Jigmet trained, and made his first feature with “The Orphanage.” He went on to direct “The Impossible,” “A Monster Calls,” “Jurassic World: Fallen Kingdom” and “Society of the Snow.” “What I find so beautiful about ‘The Dragon Letter’ is how a deeply personal story, rooted in a remote corner of the Himalayas, can speak to something universal: friendship, kindness, and the courage to find your own voice,” Bayona said. “That, to me, is the magic of cinema. It brings us together, helps us make sense of our own little worlds, and gives us a language through which we can understand one another. The more deeply we explore what makes us unique, the more we discover what connects us to the rest of the world. Sometimes, the most universal stories are born in the most unexpected places.” A BAFTA nominee who co-founded Sikhya Entertainment, the Mumbai banner, Monga Kapoor won the documentary short Oscar in 2023 alongside director Kartiki Gonsalves for “The Elephant Whisperers,” the first Indian production to take that award. She was also an executive producer on “Period. End of Sentence.,” which won in the same category in 2019. France has made her a Chevalier de l’Ordre des Arts et des Lettres, and she set up Women in Film India to support women and gender-diverse professionals in the country’s screen sector. “What moved me most about ‘The Dragon Letter’ is its beautiful message about childhood friendship. When you’re young, a friend who helps you with your homework or draws a dragon for you can make you feel understood in a way that stays with you for life. Stanzin captures that tenderness so honestly and reminds us how those small acts of kindness can give children the confidence to find their own voice. I’m delighted to come on board as executive producer and help share his film with audiences around the world,” Monga Kapoor said. For an independent filmmaker, Jigmet tells Variety , Monga Kapoor brings ties to publicists and a working knowledge of awards campaigns. “She has lots of experience and such a personality in championing this independent cinema and taking it to international stages. I’m really grateful that Guneet joined my project as an executive producer and helping us a lot,” he says. Khanna, who was raised in Amritsar, runs the kitchen at Bungalow in New York and is a judge on “MasterChef India.” He has published 36 books and made several documentaries, and his Feed India initiative has helped provide millions of meals. His first feature as director, “The Last Color,” starred Neena Gupta and centered on a friendship that grows between an older widow and a young tightrope walker in Varanasi. “I love the way he shows how children look after one another in ways adults might barely notice,” Khanna said. The story centers on Skarma (Jigmet Spalchen), a 10-year-old who is asked to pen a note to his Barcelona sponsor. Every child in the class is supposed to copy out the same text and sketch the same dragon. Skarma has other ideas about what to say. The question is whether he can summon the nerve to write them down. The film draws on Jigmet’s own years at a Himalayan boarding school. Many of his friends there had sponsors in Europe and had to send them a thank-you letter every year. Jigmet would decorate those letters with a dragon, including for classmates who helped with his schoolwork. He wrote the script at ESCAC in Barcelona, where every student on his master’s program had to pitch a story to the school. Being in Spain already suited the project, since its final section had to be filmed in Europe. Jigmet comes from Mulbekh, a Himalayan village without a cinema. “I grew up very far from the industry, so in Ladakh I learned filmmaking from YouTube only,” he says. In 2021 he launched Ladakh-based Pixel Challenger Films, making ads and public awareness films, and he also worked on Vidhu Vinod Chopra’s “12th Fail.” A few of his narrative commercials went viral, and ESCAC got in touch offering him a scholarship for a master’s in film directing. One of his professors there told the class: “Never do films with kids and dogs. You are going to struggle a lot.” Jigmet went on to write a film with 75 children in it. The Barcelona shoot, with a professional crew and professional actors, was “like a luxury for me,” he says. Ladakh was another matter. There he worked with non-actors, an entire school of children and a very small team. Equipment was scarce, and local kids pitched in by holding the lights. Having grown up in the Himalayas within that culture, Jigmet says, he was able to draw natural performances from his young cast. Jigmet lensed the Ladakh scenes himself and also edited the film. Miguel Esteban Alonso handled cinematography for the Barcelona unit. Sergi Casamitjana and Aintza Serra produced for ESCAC Films, with Pixel Challenger Films participating. Jigmet Wangial, Rosa Nicolás, Ferran Devick and Urgain Phuntsog round out the cast. Victor H. L. Bruneau was line producer, Natali Gutierrez production designer and Sebastián Orueta Murillo sound designer. Sikhya, a Jio Studios company, has backed titles including “The Lunchbox,” “Masaan,” “Pagglait” and “Kill,” along with Indian National Film Award winners “Kathal – A Jackfruit Mystery” and “Soorarai Pottru.” Its latest theatrical releases are Karthik Subbaraj’s “Dorothy” and “Udta Teer,” the first feature from writer-director Akash Kaushik. For now, Jigmet is busy with the short’s Oscar campaign. “But I’m also developing a feature version of ‘The Dragon Letter.’ That’s the plan,” he says. Jigmet is currently attending the WAVES Film Bazaar , the market component of the International Film Festival of India in Goa. A recording of sex noises appeared to be played from the audience as Strictly judge Motsi Mabuse delivered her remarks about the performance of Delta Goodrem and partner Kai Widdrington. Microphones picked up the noise. Mabuse turned to the audience to establish what was going on, before facing the camera again and exclaiming: “It’s not me.” Emma Willis had to apologise at the end of tonight’s Strictly Come Dancing for ‘anything offensive’ that was heard during the show. Turns out, it was sex noises played by someone in the background. The episode of #Strictly is currently still not available on iPlayer. pic.twitter.com/fPxDW45h1V — sᴜᴘᴇʀ ᴛᴠ (@superTV247) November 21, 2026 At the end of the show (the format on which ABC’s Dancing with the Stars is based), presenter Emma Willis apologized to viewers “if you heard any audio disruptions”. title: James Gray on Francis Ford Coppola’s Advice That Shaped His Career: ‘Be Personal. There’s Only One of You in This World’
full_text: × Nov 22, 2026 2:15am PT James Gray on Francis Ford Coppola’s Advice That Shaped His Career: ‘Be Personal. There’s Only One of You in This World’ By Essie Assibu Plus Icon Essie Assibu Latest James Gray on Francis Ford Coppola’s Advice That Shaped His Career: ‘Be Personal. There’s Only One of You in This World’ 6 hours ago ‘The Blind Ferryman’ Director on Rejecting Western Stereotypes: ‘I Don’t Want to Make a Movie Asking for Sympathy’ 1 day ago ‘Your Daughter’ Director on Bonds With Mom, Marianne Khoury, and ‘Uncle Joe,’ Youssef Chahine: ‘Filmmaking Is Really About Healing’ 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Getty Images When filmmaker James Gray was a teenager, he wrote a fan letter to Francis Ford Coppola . To his surprise, the legendary filmmaker wrote back with a piece of advice that would come to shape Gray’s entire approach to cinema. “He said, ‘Be personal, James. There’s only one of you in this world,’” Gray recalled during a press conference Sunday at the Doha Film Festival . “I’ve tried to take that to heart, that if I have anything to say at all, if I have a voice that matters at all, it’s best that I become as personal as I can.” Related Stories Cannes Condemns Five-Year Prison Sentence Against Iranian Palme d’Or Winner Jafar Panahi and Pleads for International Support Decades later, that philosophy remains central to Gray’s filmmaking, even as he argues that the film industry increasingly pressures directors to suppress their individual voices. “So much of the system, the systems in the cinema, both in the United States and abroad, try to discourage you from your own voice,” he said. “Or, if they don’t discourage you actively, they try to get you to bury your voice in a larger statement, or another form of genre, where it’s hidden.” The director was in Doha to present the MENA premiere of “ Paper Tiger ,” his latest crime drama starring Adam Driver, Miles Teller and Scarlett Johansson. Set in 1980s New York, the film follows two brothers whose pursuit of the American Dream draws them into a dangerous scheme involving the Russian mafia. Drawing heavily on his own family history, Gray described the film as an attempt to faithfully capture his father’s relationship with his uncle, while acknowledging the possible limitations of his own memory years later. He also recalled how a confrontation between his parents found its way into the film, with the actors recreating the incident almost exactly as it had unfolded in real life. Although “Paper Tiger” is framed as a crime drama, Gray said he does not think of his films primarily in terms of genre, which he sees as a way of categorizing cinema rather than defining its true purpose. “I’m just telling my story as best I can, as clearly as I can, as honestly as I can, and I hope for the best,” he said. For Gray, that commitment to honesty is also a means of fostering compassion and understanding. “That is how we extend the idea of compassion and sympathy in this world,” he explained. “Hopefully you can see something in me that matters to you.” “I have been very lucky to be able to pursue a cinema which is very directly personal,” he added. “So I don’t take it lightly. It’s a responsibility I take very seriously. And I think it’s actually the true calling of the filmmaker.” The conversation also turned to the future of independent cinema, with Brazilian producer Rodrigo Teixeira, whose “Paper Tiger” and “Furies” are both screening in Doha, pushing back against concerns about the dominance of Hollywood blockbusters. “You’re always going to have space to create original films outside of the system, because it’s impossible to own the whole system, even with all these mergers,” Teixeira said, citing companies such as A24 and Neon as examples of how independent filmmaking continues to thrive. Drawing a comparison between filmmaking in Brazil and the U.S., Teixeira argued that independent producers face much the same challenges regardless of geography. The principal difference, he said, is the public funding available in his home country, where federal support for cinema has long helped sustain the industry. “We have a government who supports cinema, who supports art,” he said, contrasting Brazil’s system with the U.S., where comparable government support is absent. Gray, meanwhile, recalled that he once believed cinema might follow the trajectory of opera, flourishing for roughly a century before eventually being eclipsed by another art form. While he acknowledged that cinema faces growing competition from video games and other forms of entertainment, and described the dominance of the blockbuster model as “overall quite harmful.” But the increasing accessibility of filmmaking technology has begun to challenge his earlier pessimism. “I have a kind of optimism about the availability of technology and how that will introduce new voices.” Lionsgate Quarterly Revenue Pops 41% on Strength of ‘Michael,’ TV Series Sales as Studio Narrows Net Loss Anthony Boyle on Becoming Sam Bankman-Fried for ‘The Altruists’ and Finding the Grey in History’s Villains: ‘I’ve Played More Real People Than Not’ ‘Nobody Wants This’ Renewed for Season 4 at Netflix ‘Big Mistakes’ Season 2 Casts Randall Park, Debi Mazar, T.R. title: SXSW Forges Partnership With Egypt’s UTH Festival Dedicated to Youth Culture
full_text: × Nov 22, 2026 1:41am PT SXSW Forges Partnership With Egypt’s UTH Festival Dedicated to Youth Culture By Nick Vivarelli Plus Icon Nick Vivarelli International Correspondent @NickVivarelli Latest Neon-Backed Biopic ‘Caesar,’ About Syrian Officer Who Blew the Whistle on Assad Regime Torture, to Be Directed by Ameer Fakher Eldin 7 hours ago Qatar’s Film Committee and Watermelon Pictures Forge Partnership to Co-Produce a Slate of Films From the ‘Global South’ 1 day ago Mel Gibson’s ‘The Resurrection of the Christ’ Bought for Italy by RAI Cinema and Leone Film Group 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy Diaa Elsadat Austin’s South by Southwest Film and TV Festival has forged a partnership with Egypt ’s UTH Festival dedicated to youth culture under which UTH will become SXSW ‘s partner in Egypt. The agreement is aimed at “identifying emerging talent and building opportunities for Egyptian filmmakers, musicians, creators, founders and business leaders to engage with SXSW’s international network,” according to a statement. Related Stories Sequels, Subtitles and Spring Releases: How the Best Picture Race Is Rewriting the Academy’s Playbook Pierce Brosnan Welcomes Robert Pattinson Into the James Bond Family: ‘You Are Going to Be Magnificent’ The third edition of the just concluded UTH Festival just ran Nov. 20 and 21 at the Grand Egyptian Museum in Giza, on the west bank of the Nile opposite Cairo, attracting roughly 10,000 attendees, according to organizers. This year’s festival, held under the theme “Work in Progress,” covered fashion, design, creator economy, film, music, food and sports, among other spheres. The announcement stems from an initiative bringing SXSW and Egyptian industry figures together during the UTH fest, which was attended by Peter Lewis, who is SXSW’s chief commercial officer. As part of the collaboration, an Egyptian delegation comprising roughly 20 participants will travel to SXSW to attend the fest between March 13–21. Curated and led by UTH, the delegation will “bring together representatives from Egypt’s film and music industries, the creator economy, entrepreneurship, investment and institutional sectors,” according to the statement. The agreement also includes plans for “a UTH-led programming session and a community gathering in Austin,” the statement added. The collaboration also envisions possible Egyptian participation in the SXSW EDU program and SXSW London in 2027, with formats to be developed by the parties. Going forward, “UTH’s ambition is to establish an Egypt House at SXSW, providing a gathering place for Egyptian talent, companies and institutional partners in Austin,” according to the statement. “SXSW was founded to help creative people connect, launch new ideas, and shape the future,” Peter Lewis said in the statement. “We are excited to partner with the UTH Festival team, who share our vision to empower the next generation of compelling, visionary and diverse creative voices,” he added. “We look forward to working closely with UTH in Egypt, and welcoming leaders from Egypt’s business, entertainment and creative industries to Austin next March.” Commented Omar El Aawar, UTH Festival founder and CEO: “Egypt has no shortage of creative talent. What we need are more opportunities for that talent to connect with the global industry.” El Aawar added: “Our partnership with SXSW is about building that bridge, creating real opportunities for Egyptian filmmakers, musicians, creators and entrepreneurs to take their work beyond our borders.” “We want UTH to be more than a festival that brings people together for two days. We want to build a platform that opens doors throughout the year, and this partnership is an important step towards that ambition.” Pictured above: Omar El Aawar, founder and CEO of UTH (seated left); Peter Lewis, chief commercial officer of SXSW (seated right). title: Neon-Backed Biopic ‘Caesar,’ About Syrian Officer Who Blew the Whistle on Assad Regime Torture, to Be Directed by Ameer Fakher Eldin
full_text: × Nov 22, 2026 1:28am PT Neon-Backed Biopic ‘Caesar,’ About Syrian Officer Who Blew the Whistle on Assad Regime Torture, to Be Directed by Ameer Fakher Eldin Syrian star Taim Hassan has been cast as the hero who provided photographic proof that the Assad regime was torturing and executing thousands of Syrians in the regime’s prisons By Nick Vivarelli Plus Icon Nick Vivarelli International Correspondent @NickVivarelli Latest SXSW Forges Partnership With Egypt’s UTH Festival Dedicated to Youth Culture 7 hours ago Neon-Backed Biopic ‘Caesar,’ About Syrian Officer Who Blew the Whistle on Assad Regime Torture, to Be Directed by Ameer Fakher Eldin 7 hours ago Qatar’s Film Committee and Watermelon Pictures Forge Partnership to Co-Produce a Slate of Films From the ‘Global South’ 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy Doha Film Festival Ameer Fakher Eldin (“The Stranger,” “Yunan”) is set to direct Neon-backed biopic “Caesar.” The film centers on Syrian military officer Farid Al-Madhhan who blew the whistle on torture and killings perpetrated by the regime of Syrian president Bashar Assad. Syrian star Taim Hassan has been cast in the lead role playing the film’s titular hero, who’s nom de guerre was Caesar. Farid Al-Madhhan was a military police photographer and head of the judicial evidence office in Damascus. Related Stories TV's Biggest Salaries: Zendaya, Nicolas Cage, Selena Gomez and More Stars Earning Huge Paychecks Robert Pattinson Trolled by U.K. Government in Youth Employment Scheme Post After Bond Reveal: He’ll ‘Apply for All 90,000 Jobs’ Al-Madhhan launched a secret operation to smuggle more than 50,000 photographs out of Syria showing evidence of torture, starvation and murder in the country’s lockups. This evidence marked a turning point in Syrian history, prompting European prosecutors to take legal proceeding against the Assad government’s war crimes. The dictator’s reign of terror ended in December 2024 after a 13-year civil war that caused more than 500,000 deaths and forced millions of Syrians to leave their homeland. Hassan has played the lead in hit Arabic TV show “Al Hayba,” about a family of arms smugglers working the border between Syria and Lebanon, a role that made him a household name across the region and reached international audiences on Netflix. His more recent work includes the show “Taj” (2024), in which he plays a boxer resisting the French occupation of Syria; hit political drama “Under the Seventh Ground” (2025); and thriller series “Mawlana” (2026). The high-end biopic was unveiled during an emotionally charged press conference held during the Industry Days of the Doha Film Festival , attended by a broad panel. The panel included both Taim Hassan, set to play Caesar, and the real Farid Al-Madhhan. (They are pictured above, from left to right) . Al-Madhhan pointed out that the upcoming film about his act – which carried extreme danger of torture and murder by Syrian authorities – will not be “a forensic or documentary exercise.” “It is a human story – the story of people who had lives, families and experiences, but whose lives unfortunately ended in inhumane circumstances. That is why we decided to tell this story through cinema: to give a voice to the human beings who suffered,” he said. “Seeing the actor and the person he is portraying sitting together is quite remarkable,” noted U.S. producer Mike Larocca, co-founder of Department M. “It is like looking in a mirror,” he added. “I think we have managed to find the right actor.” The “Caesar” project is being developed by Department M and Doha’s Katara Studios, with distribution in place via Neon and support from Kuwait-based studio Sard Media. Syrian production company Tadmor Film City is also on board. BAFTA-nominated screenwriting duo Rory Haines and Sohrab Noshirvani (“The Mauritanian,” “Informer”) are on board to write the screenplay. Berlin-based helmer Ameer Fakher Eldin, who was born in Kyiv, Ukraine, to Syrian parents from the Golan Heights, said: “Caesar’s story carries enormous responsibility. Behind the scale of the events is the deeply human story of an individual confronted with an extraordinary choice, and the courage required to act when the consequences were almost unimaginable.” The project had been first announced during the first edition of the Doha Industry Days in 2025 by the Qatar Film Committee, an official body that is part of the Media City Qatar hub tasked with driving growth of the country’s entertainment industry. Commented Hassan Al Thawadi, the Qatari lawyer who chairs the Qatar Film Committee: “Caesar’s story is one of extraordinary courage, sacrifice and global consequence. When we announced this project last year, our ambition was to assemble a cast and creative team capable of approaching his story with the humanity, sensitivity and cinematic ambition it deserves.” Larocca at the press conference noted that “it is very rare for a film of this nature to receive the level of resources and support that we have received.” He thanked Al Thawadi and the other partners “for giving us the support necessary to attempt to make a film of the highest possible quality by international standards.” “I hope we will be back here next year to announce significant production milestones,” he said. title: Karla Sofia Gascon Says ‘Emilia Perez’ Oscar Controversy Came From People Who ‘Didn’t Want Someone Like Me to Receive an Award’
full_text: × Nov 21, 2026 11:39pm PT Karla Sofia Gascon Says ‘Emilia Perez’ Oscar Controversy Came From People Who ‘Didn’t Want Someone Like Me to Receive an Award’ By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest J.A. Bayona, Guneet Monga Kapoor, Vikas Khanna Board Student Academy Award Winner ‘The Dragon Letter’ as Director Plans Feature Version (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago Karla Sofia Gascon Says ‘Emilia Perez’ Oscar Controversy Came From People Who ‘Didn’t Want Someone Like Me to Receive an Award’ 9 hours ago Oscar-Winning Doc ‘The Elephant Whisperers’ Co-Writer’s Dark Comedy ‘Nose Bone’ Follows a Punjabi Woman’s Race for an Abortion at WAVES Film Bazaar 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source PIB Spanish actor Karla Sofia Gascon , whose turn in “Emilia Pérez” made her the first transgender actor to land an Oscar nomination, says the controversy that consumed her awards campaign was driven by people who did not want to see someone like her win. “In reality, the controversy was generated by a great many people who didn’t want someone like me to receive an award,” Gascón tells Variety at the International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa, where her Spanish Western “Trinidad” is world premiering. Related Stories Robert Pattinson Said in 2012 That He'd 'Definitely' Want to Be James Bond in 'Like 20 Years' When He's Not So 'Fresh-Faced' From a Mockbuster Version of 'The Odyssey' to a 'Jiu-Jitsu Nun': How Producers Are Keeping the Low-Budget Film Market Alive Via Streaming (and Even Lower Budgets) Her Oscar run was overshadowed by a row over old social media posts . “It has never yet been shown that I wrote anything against anyone, nor has it been proven anywhere,” she says. “It was just a pile of assumptions, with everyone saying something different, and they created a figure of me that isn’t me.” Gascon describes a long awards push as an ordeal for actors, with political interests at play on every side, and says she would rather do her work and let audiences decide whether they like it. Such campaigns, she argues, open the door to people using actors for political or economic ends. “And I think we are here for the art,” she says. Cinema, in her view, carries a social responsibility to show audiences the best of humanity, even as it remains both entertainment and business. Mixing the political, the economic and the talent, she says, dilutes the essence of acting, which for her means bringing lives to other people and making them think. Transgender people face more and more problems, Gascón says. “We are living through a moment of regression in the rights of transgender people, of sexual diversity.” Global politics, Gascon adds, is making life harder still for people who already face steep odds, and above all for trans people, “who are considered in practically the whole world as the lowest in society.” That, she says, is why a campaign arose against “a woman who could win a great award” – a reading she stresses is “not a justification” but “an explanation.” “ Emilia Perez ,” directed by Jacques Audiard , won Gascon best actress at the Cannes Film Festival, the European Film Awards and the Lumiere Awards, alongside Golden Globe and BAFTA nominations. The biggest change to her career since, she says, is that she no longer has to audition. “I started at 16, I’ve had a career of more than 30 years and I’ve done everything in acting,” she says. She has since made the Italian film “Scuola di Seduzione” and “Trinidad.” On working across languages and cultures, she says: “It makes me grow as a person, it makes me grow in my work, it makes me understand human beings much more.” Next up is “Las Malas,” Armando Bo’s adaptation of Camila Sosa Villada’s novel, in which she plays Tia Encarna and which she rates among the best work of her life. The film shot for around four months this year in Argentina and Uruguay. Gascon sees many parallels with “Emilia Perez” in the role but would rather discuss it once audiences have seen it, possibly at Cannes or Venice. During a masterclass at the festival, where she was honored by Chanchal Kumar, secretary of India’s Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, Gascon detailed her “Trinidad” character: a gun-wielding outlaw who uses a wheelchair and serves as the villain of the 19th-century tale. She had hoped for horses and guns when the Western came calling, only to learn she would be playing a woman “in a chair without any movement.” “And when you confront this, you say, ‘That’s the best opportunity for me to understand other people in this world,'” she told the audience. Gascon builds every role from the voice outward, seeking a “really soft, really calm” register for the “Trinidad” role. On “Emilia Pérez,” she recorded a range of voices on cassette before settling on a deep voice for Manitas and a “delicate” one for Emilia, and came to appreciate the process when dubbing herself later. She called Audiard the best director she has worked with. “He brings you the liberty to act,” Gascón said. “He plays a lot, he laughs a lot, he’s really funny, and I think he is a really good friend.” On set, she said, actors should remember they are one part of a team that can run to hundreds. “I don’t want to create conflict on set. I don’t want to create a difference between me and the others. I don’t want blue flowers in my caravan,” she said. Gascon traced her affection for India to a Madrid screening of Deepa Mehta’s “Water” decades ago, and named Indian Oscar winner A.R. Rahman her favorite musician. She also drew parallels between the heightened performance styles of Mexican telenovelas, where she spent much of her career, and Indian cinema, arguing that histrionics and truth are compatible. She also said filmmakers too often cast to labels such as “Spanish” or “she is a woman” instead of trusting actors’ range. “It’s nice when Indian people work in Spain, work in the United States. Discussing the fourth and final season with Deadline, Ashley Lyle and Bart Nickerson explained that they didn’t want to “run the risk of overstaying our welcome” with another season when they were reaching the conclusion “more rapidly.” “We’d always said that we had pitched a five-season plan, but we’d always given the caveat that we felt like the show would tell us when it wanted to end, and just in the breaking of this story, it started to feel like we were sort of moving towards the end more rapidly,” explained Nickerson. “And so, then the decision kind of became, ‘OK, do we sort of squeeze a lot into Season 4 or run the risk of overstaying our welcome out of the fifth season?’ We chose to try to squeeze it in, and that ended up really just kind of working out nicely from our perspective. title: Russell Brand Selling “Free Russell” Merch Via His Wellness Business While in Prison
full_text: × Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All November 21, 2026 4:16pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Russell Brand photographed arriving at Southwark Crown Court. Courtesy of Getty Russell Brand is selling merchandise calling for his freedom while he’s behind bars after being sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison after being found guilty of rape and sexual assault. It is unclear how long the items have been available for purchase on Reborn, however the earliest reviews on the varying products date to Nov. 16 (he was sentenced Nov. 9). Brand recently received backlash for sharing a message from prison , delivered by his wife, Laura Brand, on his YouTube channel where he claimed he was innocent. Related Stories News Google Says It's Investigating Russell Brand YouTube Video Where He Said He's "Not Guilty" in Message From Prison News Over 400 U.K. Industry Figures Demand End to "Culture of Open Secrets" After Russell Brand Trial “So Russell has asked me to read something to you today,” the actor’s wife said at the start of the video, before looking to a notebook to read her husband’s message. “Beloved brothers and sisters in Christ, God bless you for your support. As you know, I am not guilty for the offenses I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening.” Brand was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison after being found guilty of rape and sexual assault. The trial lasted four weeks at Southwark Crown Court, with the jury finding him guilty on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault (he was found not guilty on two other rape charges and not guilty of attempted indecent assault). The actor has three items featuring “Free Russell” available for purchase on the website for Reborn, his wellness business. Every item is available for $34.99; a shirt with the words “Free Russell Brand “; a hat with the same text; and another shirt that reads “Free Russell” with an image of himself. Upon visiting the Reborn website, images of the merch are displayed on its homepage with text that reads, “Stand with Russell against injustice” and “silenced for speaking out.” After clicking on the “Free Russell” section of the site, the items are labeled as “fundraiser apparel,” with a descriptor that additionally reads, “Silenced for speaking out against injustuce and corruption.” After the YouTube video was shared, Google, the parent company of YouTube, told BBC News it was “aware of the new content and our teams are investigating,” adding, “We suspended Russell Brand’s channel from the YouTube Partner Program in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetise on YouTube since then.” BBC News also reported that Google declined a request from the Ministry of Justice to remove the video, saying none of its rules had been broken. His message, delivered by his wife in the YouTube video, drew criticism, with Britain’s Justice Secretary Alex Norris calling the broadcast of a statement from Brand while he is behind bars “completely unacceptable.” “Prisoners are rightly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims,” Norris wrote on X. “This is being urgently investigated, and I expect action to be taken if he is found to have broken the rules.” THR

At the time, it was described as a new interpretation of Ellis’ novel rather than a remake of the original film. “We are thrilled to add another elite filmmaker to our upcoming slate,” Lionsgate Motion Picture Group chair Adam Fogelson said in a statement at the time. “Luca is a brilliant artist, and the perfect visionary to create a whole new interpretation of this potent and classic IP.” The original 2000 film starred Christian Bale as Patrick Bateman, an investment banker living a secret life as a serial killer.
